what_its_for: Fulvestrant is used to treat hormone receptor-positive (HR+) breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. It works by blocking estrogen receptors in the body, which slows or stops the growth of certain breast cancer cells that need estrogen to grow. It may be used alone or with other cancer medicines.
how_to_take: Fulvestrant is given as two injections (shots) into the muscle of your buttocks, one on each side. These injections are always given by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting — you will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each injection is given slowly over 1 to 2 minutes. You will usually receive both injections on the same day.
dosing: The usual dose is 500 mg (two 250 mg injections) given on Day 1, Day 15, and Day 29 of treatment, and then once every month (every 28 days) after that. Always follow the schedule your doctor gives you. Try not to miss or delay your appointments.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your injection appointment, call your doctor's office or clinic as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Do not wait until your next regularly scheduled dose. Your doctor will decide the best time to give you your next injection.
storage: Fulvestrant is stored and handled by your healthcare team at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. At the clinic, it is kept in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and protected from light. It should never be frozen.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor before starting fulvestrant if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control (non-hormonal methods such as condoms) during treatment and for at least 1 year after your last dose. Avoid hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings) as they may interfere with your treatment. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially blood thinners like warfarin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: unusual pain, redness, swelling, or bruising at the injection site; signs of a blood clot such as sudden leg pain, swelling, warmth, or redness in one leg, or sudden chest pain and shortness of breath; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; bone pain that is new or gets worse; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; hot flashes or other side effects that bother you; or if you think you may be pregnant.
when_it_works: Fulvestrant does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before your doctor can tell if the medicine is working. Your doctor will check your progress with regular exams, blood tests, and imaging scans (such as CT scans or bone scans). Keep all your follow-up appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use fulvestrant if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. It can cause serious harm to an unborn baby or a nursing infant. Liver problems: If you have moderate or severe liver disease, your doctor may adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Older adults: Fulvestrant can be used in older women; no dose adjustment is usually needed based on age alone. Children: Fulvestrant is not approved for use in children.
